faq.q: Why does the temperature stay at 100 °C while rice cooks?
faq.a: Water boils at about 100 degrees at sea level, and while it is boiling, extra heat turns water into steam instead of raising the temperature. So the pot bottom stays steady until the water is gone.
asks: How does a rice cooker know when to stop?

faq.q: How does the magnet switch work?
faq.a: A spring-loaded magnet sits against the pot. It is made of a ferrite that loses its magnetism when it gets hotter than about 103 degrees. When that happens, the spring pulls it away and flips the switch.
asks: What is the thermostat in a rice cooker?

faq.q: Why does a rice cooker switch to keep warm?
faq.a: Once the main heater is switched off, a small low-power heater keeps the rice warm without burning it.
asks: What does keep warm mean on a rice cooker?

faq.q: Why must you use the right amount of water?
faq.a: The cooker stops when the water is gone. Too little water and it stops before the rice is soft; too much and the rice turns mushy before the water runs out.

faq.q: Do all rice cookers work this way?
faq.a: Simple ones do. Fancier ones use temperature sensors and a microchip, sometimes called fuzzy logic, to adjust the heat for different types of rice.
asks: What is a fuzzy logic rice cooker?

facts: Toshiba launched the first widely sold automatic electric rice cooker in Japan in 1955.
Simple rice cookers switch off when the pot bottom rises above about 103 °C, which can only happen once the free water is gone.
